name: Discord Cache & Code Cache
whatIsIt: Discord stores a local copy of every video, audio message, GIF, image, and emoji loaded across your servers and direct messages.
whatHappens: Deleting this clears disk space immediately. It does NOT delete your chat history, server memberships, Krisp noise suppression settings, server layouts, or account credentials. Discord simply re-downloads media as you view it.
manualSteps: Completely exit Discord (right-click the Discord icon in your system tray and select 'Quit Discord').
Press the Windows Key + R to open the Run dialog.
Type %appdata%\discord and hit Enter.
Delete the folders named 'Cache', 'Code Cache', and 'GPUCache'.

customFaqs.q: Will deleting %AppData%\Discord\Cache_Data log me out or delete my Discord messages?
customFaqs.a: No. All Discord messages and server history live on Discord's cloud servers, and your session token is stored separately. Clearing Cache_Data, Code Cache, and GPUCache frees disk space and fixes laggy server switching.

customFaqs.q: Why does Discord store gigabytes inside Cache_Data and Code Cache on Windows 11?
customFaqs.a: Discord is built on Electron/Chromium and aggressively caches server images, embedded videos, voice waveforms, and JS bytecode in %AppData%\discord. Purging Cache, Code Cache, and GPUCache restores 1.5–6 GB without touching Local Storage tokens.

name: Windows.old (Previous Windows Installation)
whatIsIt: C:\Windows.old is the full snapshot archive created during a Windows 10-to-11 upgrade or annual feature update (such as 23H2 to 24H2), holding your previous OS Windows, Program Files, and Users directories under TrustedInstaller permissions so the 'Go back' recovery option remains available for 10 days.
whatHappens: Once the 10-day upgrade rollback window expires—or once you confirm your upgraded PC runs smoothly—removing 'Previous Windows installation(s)' via Windows Storage Settings or SWEEPR Cleaner safely reclaims 15 GB to 35 GB of primary SSD storage without touching your active Documents or apps.
manualSteps: Open Settings → System → Storage → Temporary files.
Check 'Previous Windows installation(s)' and click 'Remove files'.
Alternative if Storage Settings doesn't clear it: open Start, search Disk Cleanup, click 'Clean up system files' (Admin), check 'Previous Windows installation(s)', and click OK.
Verify C:\Windows.old is gone—avoid using takeown/icacls manually unless Disk Cleanup fails completely.

customFaqs.q: Why can't I delete C:\Windows.old directly in File Explorer?
customFaqs.a: C:\Windows.old is owned by the TrustedInstaller system account and contains thousands of hard-linked system binaries. Use Settings -> System -> Storage -> Temporary files ('Previous Windows installation(s)') or SWEEPR Cleaner to remove it cleanly.

customFaqs.q: Why is Windows.old (Previous Windows Installation) taking up so much disk space on Windows 11?
customFaqs.a: When Windows upgrades to a major new version or build, it saves a complete backup of your previous OS files in C:\Windows.old so you can roll back. Clearing it typically reclaims 15.0 GB safely.

customFaqs.q: Does clearing Windows.old (Previous Windows Installation) delete personal saves or logins?
customFaqs.a: No. If your PC has been running smoothly for more than 10 days after an update, deleting Windows.old is completely safe and reclaims 20+ GB.

customFaqs.q: Is it safe to delete Windows.old folder?
customFaqs.a: Yes, once your Windows 11 upgrade or 24H2 feature update has run stably and you do not plan to roll back to your previous OS build, removing C:\Windows.old safely reclaims 15–35 GB without affecting personal files.

customFaqs.q: Can I delete Windows.old after 10 days?
customFaqs.a: Yes. Windows 10 and 11 only allow 'Go back' rollbacks for 10 days after a feature upgrade anyway—after 10 days the rollback expires automatically, so deleting 'Previous Windows installation(s)' is recommended to free SSD space.

customFaqs.q: How do I force delete Windows.old if Access Denied?
customFaqs.a: File Explorer blocks direct deletion because TrustedInstaller owns C:\Windows.old. Instead open Settings -> System -> Storage -> Temporary files and check 'Previous Windows installation(s)', or run cleanmgr as Administrator and select 'Previous Windows installation(s)'.

name: NVIDIA DirectX Shader Cache (DXCache)
whatIsIt: NVIDIA's graphics driver stores compiled DirectX 11 and DirectX 12 shader binaries in DXCache so games load faster without stuttering.

customFaqs.q: Is it safe to clear NVIDIA shader cache?

customFaqs.a: Leave Shader Cache Size enabled (Driver Default or 10 GB) in NVIDIA Control Panel so games do not stutter recompiling shaders every session, and periodically clear obsolete shader generations inside DXCache to reclaim SSD space.

questionTitle: Can I delete NVIDIA DXCache? Does clearing shader cache fix game stuttering?
directAnswer: Yes—%LocalAppData%\NVIDIA\DXCache is safe to clear and frees 2–14 GB without touching your NVIDIA Control Panel settings or game saves. Clearing a bloated or corrupted shader cache after GPU driver updates often fixes persistent frame-time spikes, at the cost of brief shader recompilation on each game's first launch.
whenNotToDelete: Expect 1–3 minutes of slightly higher CPU usage or brief shader compilation stutters the first time you reopen DirectX 12 games after clearing DXCache. Skip any files currently locked by dwm.exe or running apps—that is normal.
whyItGrows: NVIDIA drivers compile hardware-specific DirectX 11/12 Pipeline State Objects (PSOs) into .bin and .toc cache files inside %LocalAppData%\NVIDIA\DXCache. Across dozens of games and driver updates, stale caches accumulate up to your driver's Shader Cache Size limit (often 10 GB or Unlimited).

shellCommand.label: PowerShell: Measure current NVIDIA DXCache footprint (Read-Only)
shellCommand.code:
$p = "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\NVIDIA\DXCache"
Get-ChildItem $p -Recurse -Force -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Measure-Object Length -Sum | Select-Object Count, @{N='SizeGB';E={[math]::Round($_.Sum/1GB,2)}}

name: Steam depotcache Folder (C:\Program Files (x86)\Steam\depotcache)
whatIsIt: What is Steam depotcache? The Steam depotcache folder stores encrypted delta-patch manifest chunks (.depot and .manifest files) used by Steam to verify and assemble game updates. When a game update is interrupted, cancelled, or uninstalled mid-patch, gigabytes of orphaned depot chunks remain locked in C:\Program Files (x86)\Steam\depotcache indefinitely.
whatHappens: Yes, Steam depotcache is 100% safe to delete as long as all current game updates have finished installing. Deleting it immediately reclaims 2 GB to 25 GB+ of SSD space without touching your installed games or Steam Cloud saves.
manualSteps: Open Steam -> View -> Downloads and verify that zero game updates are currently downloading or queued/paused.
Exit Steam completely (Steam menu -> Exit) so steam.exe releases file locks on the depotcache directory.
Open File Explorer and navigate to C:\Program Files (x86)\Steam\depotcache (or your custom Steam library folder).
Select all .depot and .manifest files (Ctrl + A) and press Shift + Delete, or use SWEEPR Cleaner to clean Steam depotcache, shadercache, and orphaned downloading folders in one click.
warning: Only delete depotcache when no Steam game downloads or patches are actively paused in your Steam Download Manager.

customFaqs.q: Will deleting Steam depotcache uninstall my games?
customFaqs.a: No. Installed games live in steamapps\common. The depotcache folder only holds temporary delta-patch manifests and encrypted pre-load staging chunks. Just make sure no game download is actively paused before cleaning.

customFaqs.q: Does cleaning Steam shader cache fix micro-stuttering?
customFaqs.a: Yes. Clearing corrupted or outdated Vulkan/DirectX shader binaries forces Steam and your GPU driver to compile a clean shader pipeline for your current driver version.

customFaqs.a: Yes, 100% safe. This folder only stores staging cab and esd packages for completed or pending Windows Updates. Deleting them reclaims 2–25 GB and forces Windows Update to fetch clean delta packages if an update was stuck.

customFaqs.q: Why is Windows Update Download Cache (SoftwareDistribution\Download) taking up so much disk space on Windows 11?

name: Windows Hibernation File (C:\hiberfil.sys)
warning: Do not delete hiberfil.sys manually. Use 'powercfg /h off' or '/h /type reduced' if you do not use Hibernate on a desktop PC.
whatIsIt: Windows reserves 40% of your total RAM size on your C: drive for C:\hiberfil.sys to support Hibernate and Fast Startup.
whatHappens: On desktop PCs with NVMe SSDs that never use Hibernate, shrinking or disabling hiberfil.sys reclaims 12–32 GB instantly.
manualSteps: Right-click the Start button and open Terminal (Admin) or Command Prompt (Admin).
To remove C:\hiberfil.sys completely, run: powercfg.exe /hibernate off and press Enter.
If you want to keep Fast Startup while cutting the file size roughly in half, run: powercfg.exe /h /type reduced instead.
You can restore hibernation at any time by running powercfg.exe /hibernate on.

customFaqs.q: Why can't I delete C:\hiberfil.sys directly in File Explorer?
customFaqs.a: Windows locks C:\hiberfil.sys while Hibernation is enabled. Running powercfg -h off in an elevated terminal (or using SWEEPR Cleaner) disables hibernation and instructs the Windows kernel to delete the 6–32 GB file immediately.

customFaqs.q: What is the difference between powercfg /h off and powercfg /h /type reduced?
customFaqs.a: Running powercfg /h /type reduced shrinks C:\hiberfil.sys by roughly half while keeping Windows Fast Startup working. Running powercfg /h off removes the entire 6–32 GB file completely, ideal for desktop PCs that never Hibernate.

questionTitle: Is C:\Windows\LiveKernelReports\WATCHDOG safe to delete?
directAnswer: Yes—the .dmp and .etl crash dump files inside C:\Windows\LiveKernelReports\WATCHDOG are safe to delete once you no longer need them for debugging, reclaiming 1.5–10 GB. Delete the dump files inside the subfolders rather than removing the C:\Windows\LiveKernelReports root directory itself.
whenNotToDelete: Hold off on deleting the newest WATCHDOG-*.dmp if you are actively troubleshooting recurring black screens or GPU driver resets (VIDEO_TDR_FAILURE in nvlddmkm.sys or amdkmdag.sys)—inspect it with WinDbg or WhoCrashed and verify GPU stability first. Administrator rights are required, and recently written dumps stay locked briefly.
whyItGrows: When Windows Display Driver Model (WDDM) recovers from a GPU timeout (TDR) or power-controller stall without triggering a full BSOD, the kernel writes uncompressed .dmp memory dumps and .etl traces into C:\Windows\LiveKernelReports\WATCHDOG, PDC, and WlanHost. Individual WATCHDOG dumps routinely reach 500 MB–2 GB each and never auto-purge quickly.

questionTitle: Can I delete the Stremio cache folder on Windows?
directAnswer: Yes. You can safely delete files inside Stremio's stremio-cache directory after quitting the app, or set a hard cap (2 GB, 5 GB, or 10 GB) under Stremio Settings → Streaming → Caching. Your library, add-ons, and watch history are synced to your Stremio account.
whenNotToDelete: Close Stremio and its background stremio-server process before clearing files so you do not interrupt an active video stream.
whyItGrows: Stremio buffers downloaded video pieces locally in stremio-cache while streaming. If Caching is set to 10 GB or Infinite in Settings → Streaming, watched movies and episodes stay on your SSD until manually cleared or overwritten.

questionTitle: System & Reserved storage taking 80–100 GB+ on Windows 11: How to shrink it
directAnswer: Windows 11 lumps five separate items into 'System & Reserved': the core OS (~25–35 GB), System Restore shadow copies, hiberfil.sys (equal to 40–100% of your RAM), pagefile.sys virtual memory, and Reserved Storage (~7 GB). You can safely reclaim 15–60 GB by trimming System Restore points, disabling hibernation if unused, and running DISM component cleanup.
whenNotToDelete: Never manually delete pagefile.sys or disable virtual memory entirely—doing so causes out-of-memory app crashes even on 32 GB PCs. Only disable hibernation if you don't use Hibernate or Fast Startup.
whyItGrows: On systems with 32–64 GB of RAM, hiberfil.sys and pagefile.sys alone can occupy 30–50 GB. Add unmanaged Volume Shadow Copy restore points (which can quietly hold 20–40 GB) and unpruned WinSxS update components, and Windows Settings displays 100 GB+ under System & Reserved.

name: macOS System Data Storage Bloat
warning: Never delete /System or active databases inside ~/Library/Application Support. Always inspect specific cache folders and thin Time Machine local snapshots using macOS's built-in tmutil command.
questionTitle: Mac 'System Data' taking 100 GB+? How to find and clear it safely
directAnswer: macOS groups local Time Machine APFS snapshots, ~/Library/Caches, Xcode DerivedData, orphaned iOS backups, and leftover app support files under 'System Data'. First wait 24 hours plugged-in if you just updated macOS, then thin local snapshots with tmutil and inspect ~/Library for multi-gigabyte caches to safely reclaim 20–150+ GB.
whenNotToDelete: Do not delete anything inside /System, /Library/Keychains, or active app folders in ~/Library/Application Support (such as mail, notes, or password vaults). If System Data spiked right after a macOS Sequoia/Tahoe upgrade, leave your Mac plugged in overnight so Spotlight and APFS maintenance can auto-reclaim purgeable space.
whyItGrows: Apple's System Settings → General → Storage screen does not break down what sits inside System Data. In practice, four culprits account for most 100 GB+ cases reported on r/MacOS: automatic APFS Time Machine local snapshots (created even if you rarely plug in a backup drive), Xcode DerivedData and old iOS Simulator runtimes (50–200 GB for developers), stuck iCloud Drive sync caches, and orphaned app folders inside ~/Library/Caches and ~/Library/Application Support/MobileSync/Backup.
whatIsIt: macOS System Data aggregates purgeable APFS Time Machine local snapshots, user/system app caches in ~/Library/Caches, developer build caches (~/Library/Developer), sandbox containers, and orphaned iOS device backups.
whatHappens: Thinning local APFS snapshots with tmutil and clearing verified cache/Xcode/backup leftovers frees 20–150+ GB without touching your personal Documents, Desktop, Photos library, or macOS system files.
metaTitle: Mac System Data Huge (100 GB+)? Safe Cleanup Guide
metaDescription: Mac System Data taking 100 GB+? Clear APFS Time Machine snapshots with tmutil, clean ~/Library/Caches, Xcode DerivedData & orphaned backups safely.

shellCommand.label: macOS Terminal: List & thin local Time Machine snapshots, then inspect ~/Library size
shellCommand.code:
# 1. Check local APFS Time Machine snapshots
tmutil listlocalsnapshots /

# 2. Safely thin local snapshots (asks macOS to release purgeable space)
tmutil thinlocalsnapshots / 999999999999 4

# 3. Inspect largest folders inside ~/Library (read-only)
du -sh ~/Library/* 2>/dev/null | sort -hr | head -n 15

manualSteps: If System Data jumped right after a macOS update or large file deletion, leave your Mac plugged in and idle overnight—macOS background indexing often shrinks purgeable System Data automatically.
Open Terminal and run 'tmutil listlocalsnapshots /'. If snapshots are listed, run 'tmutil thinlocalsnapshots / 999999999999 4' to release gigabytes of invisible APFS snapshot space.

In Finder, press Cmd + Shift + G, go to ~/Library/Caches, and clear cache folders for closed apps (browsers, Spotify, Adobe, Slack). Never delete the ~/Library/Caches folder itself—only contents inside specific app subfolders.
Check ~/Library/Application Support/MobileSync/Backup for forgotten old iPhone/iPad backups, and check ~/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData & CoreSimulator if you use Xcode.
If iCloud Drive sync caches are stuck, toggle System Settings → [Your Name] → iCloud → iCloud Drive off, restart your Mac, and turn it back on.

Application HTTP caches, thumbnails, and temporary browser/media buffers.
Compiled Xcode build artifacts and old iOS/iPadOS Simulator runtimes.
Local encrypted/unencrypted iPhone & iPad backups you no longer need.
macOS OS volume, Keychains, Apple Mail, and live application user data.

customFaqs.q: Why does Mac System Data keep growing back after I delete files?
customFaqs.a: Deleting large files on APFS does not free space immediately if a local Time Machine snapshot still references those blocks. Running 'tmutil thinlocalsnapshots / 999999999999 4' or waiting for macOS idle maintenance releases those blocks.

customFaqs.q: Is it safe to delete everything in ~/Library/Caches on macOS?
customFaqs.a: Close running apps first and delete only individual app cache folders you recognize rather than the ~/Library/Caches parent folder itself. macOS and your apps recreate needed caches cleanly on relaunch.

name: iPhone System Data & Duplicate Photo Bloat
path: Settings → General → iPhone Storage → System Data
questionTitle: iPhone 'System Data' taking 40 GB+? How to clear it without a factory reset
directAnswer: You can usually reclaim 10–40+ GB of iPhone System Data without wiping your phone by deleting and reinstalling cache-heavy social apps (Instagram, TikTok, Discord, Telegram), clearing Safari website data, and connecting your iPhone to a Mac or PC via Finder/iTunes to flush stuck update and sync caches.
whenNotToDelete: Before trying any aggressive cache reset or toggling Message history, check Settings → Apps → Messages → Keep Messages is set to 'Forever' if you want to keep old texts, and make sure you know your login credentials before deleting and reinstalling social apps.
whyItGrows: iOS classifies streaming caches, stuck photo-indexing buffers, unfinished iOS update payloads, and unmanaged media caches from apps like Instagram, TikTok, Spotify, and Discord inside 'System Data'. On top of that, Apple's built-in Photos 'Duplicates' album only catches byte-identical copies—leaving thousands of near-identical burst shots, blurry frames, and screenshots taking up gigabytes.
whatIsIt: iPhone System Data holds iOS system caches, Siri voices, logs, interrupted OTA update files, and temporary media caches generated by social and messaging apps.
whatHappens: Reinstalling bloated apps, flushing Safari caches, and syncing through Finder/iTunes safely drops System Data without erasing your photos, contacts, or iCloud data.
metaTitle: iPhone System Data Full (40 GB+)? Clear Without Reset
metaDescription: iPhone System Data taking 40 GB+? Shrink bloated app caches, flush Finder/iTunes temp files, and clean burst photos without a factory reset.
manualSteps: Open Settings → General → iPhone Storage, scroll to the bottom, and note your exact System Data size plus the top 5 largest apps.
Clear Safari cache: Settings → Apps → Safari → Clear History and Website Data (note: this signs you out of Safari web sessions).

Delete and reinstall (not just 'Offload') your biggest social/chat cache hogs—Instagram, TikTok, Discord, YouTube, and Telegram often hide 5–20 GB of unpurgeable cache that drops to <300 MB after a fresh reinstall.
Plug your iPhone into a Mac (Finder) or Windows PC (Apple Devices / iTunes) and trigger a local sync or check for updates—desktop sync reliably clears stuck iOS deployment caches.
Clean burst photos, blurry shots, and large screen recordings in Photos (or use SWEEPR Cleaner for iPhone to automatically keep the sharpest shot in each burst while merging duplicate contacts).

customFaqs.q: Does 'Offload App' clear iPhone app cache?
customFaqs.a: No. Offloading removes only the app binary while intentionally preserving its Documents & Data cache. To actually shrink a 10 GB Instagram or TikTok cache, choose 'Delete App' and reinstall it from the App Store.

customFaqs.q: Does the iPhone date-change trick actually work for System Data?
customFaqs.a: Advancing the clock can temporarily trigger iOS cache expiry, but it risks deleting expiring iMessages and often bounces back within days. Reinstalling bloated apps and syncing with a Mac/PC via Finder is far safer and more reliable.

name: Android 'Other' & 'System' Storage Bloat (Samsung & Pixel)
questionTitle: Android 'Other' or 'System' storage full on Samsung & Pixel: How to clear it
directAnswer: Most bloated 'Other' storage on Android comes from three hidden places: an unemptied hidden Android/.Trash folder (20–60 GB), uncategorized app data on Samsung One UI (fixed by granting Storage Usage Access), and WhatsApp/Telegram auto-downloaded media caches. Clearing these reclaims 10–50+ GB without deleting personal photos.
whenNotToDelete: Do not clear 'Storage / Clear Data' inside Android App Info for banking, authenticator, or unbacked-up messaging apps—use 'Clear Cache' instead so you keep logins and local chat databases intact.
whyItGrows: On Samsung Galaxy phones, Android lumps app data into 'Other' or 'System' until you grant Usage Access to Settings → Device Care → Storage. Meanwhile, gallery apps and file managers frequently move deleted videos into hidden .Trash folders for 30 days, and WhatsApp/Telegram silently cache gigabytes of forwarded videos and voice notes.
whatIsIt: Android 'Other' and 'System' storage buckets capture hidden trash folders, miscategorized app data without Usage Access permission, offline media downloads, and system cache partitions.
whatHappens: Enabling Usage Access, emptying hidden trash folders, and clearing app caches reclaims 10–50+ GB safely without touching your camera roll originals or installed apps.
metaTitle: Android Other Storage Full? Clear Hidden Trash & Cache
metaDescription: Android Other or System storage full on Samsung or Pixel? Fix hidden Android/.Trash, One UI Usage Access, and WhatsApp/Telegram caches safely.
manualSteps: On Samsung One UI: open Settings → Device Care → Storage → tap the info ('i') icon next to Apps and grant Usage Access. This immediately re-indexes miscategorized 'Other' storage so you can see which apps actually hold the data.

Empty every Recycle Bin / Trash: check Google Photos → Library → Trash, Samsung Gallery → Trash, My Files → Trash, and open Files by Google with 'Show hidden files' enabled to check Internal Storage → Android → .Trash.

Clear messenger media bloat: open WhatsApp → Settings → Storage and Data → Manage Storage (and Telegram → Settings → Data and Storage → Storage Usage) to clear cached forwarded videos without losing text chats.
Clear safe app caches: go to Settings → Apps → sort by Size → open media-heavy apps (Chrome, TikTok, Spotify, YouTube) → Storage → tap 'Clear Cache' (NOT 'Clear Data').

If Samsung 'System' storage remains bloated after an OS update, power off, connect USB-C to a PC, hold Volume Up + Power into Recovery Mode, choose 'Wipe Cache Partition' (does not erase personal data), and reboot.

subLocations.role: Hidden 30-day trash folders retaining deleted 4K videos and screenshots.
Forwarded videos, GIFs, and cached channel media stored locally.

subLocations.subPath: App Caches (Chrome, TikTok, Instagram, Spotify, Maps)
subLocations.role: Temporary media and offline preview files cleared via Clear Cache.

customFaqs.q: Does 'Wipe Cache Partition' on Samsung delete my photos or apps?
customFaqs.a: No. Wiping the cache partition in Recovery Mode only removes temporary OS update logs and cached system files. Never choose 'Wipe data/factory reset', which erases the phone.

customFaqs.q: Why does Samsung Storage say 'Other' is 40 GB even after I delete apps?
customFaqs.a: Either Usage Access is turned off for My Files / Storage (causing app data to show under 'Other'), or deleted videos are still sitting in Gallery Trash or hidden Android/.Trash for 30 days.
